yt_description:
The whole valley laughed when Rosa let beavers dam her creek… until the drought came. 🦫💧
Beaver dams slow a stream down so the water soaks into the ground like a sponge. In Elko County, Nevada, ranchers who let beavers return saw more water in their creeks, later into the dry season and even in drought years. (Rosa is a fictional character; the beavers are real science.)

Sources: Charnley (2019), USDA Forest Service PNW-RP-614 "If You Build It, They Will Come"; Fairfax & Small (2018) on Nevada beaver dams; Medill News "Beavers help battle ongoing drought".

script: This rancher lets a family of beavers move into her creek. And the whole valley thinks she has lost her mind. Out here in the desert, water is everything. Every summer, the creeks shrink to dust. Her neighbor digs a deeper well and hauls water in a big tank. It costs a fortune. But Rosa fences her cows away from the creek, so the willows can grow back on the banks. Then one morning, a beaver shows up. The valley laughs. Beavers? They'll flood your whole ranch! Rosa does something even stranger. She lets them stay. Even when they chew down her willows to build dams. The valley laughs even louder. She's letting rodents run her ranch! Rosa just smiles. And waits. Dam by dam, the creek slows down. The water spreads out and soaks into the ground, like a giant sponge. Then the big drought comes. The neighbor's creek turns to cracked mud. But Rosa's creek is still full. Green grass, ducks, fish, and plenty of water for her cows. That night, the neighbor knocks on her door. Rosa... how do I get some beavers? Beavers really do this. In the Nevada desert, ranchers who let beavers come back found more water in their creeks, even in drought years.
